title: Grammar & Composition
description: Grammar & Composition builds the sentence-level and paragraph-level skills behind clear writing: the parts of speech, sentence structure and common errors, the punctuation and capitalization rules that trip up even confident writers, and the paragraph and process skills that turn ideas into finished prose. Every lesson ends with real sentences fixed, combined, or built from scratch.
outcomes: You can identify the parts of speech and use them correctly in your own sentences.
You can distinguish simple, compound, and complex sentences, and fix fragments and run-ons.
You can apply the core rules of comma, apostrophe, quotation mark, and capitalization use.
You can build a unified paragraph around a clear topic sentence with strong supporting details.
You can move a piece of writing through prewriting, drafting, revising, and editing.
You can revise your own sentences for precise word choice, appropriate tone, and concision.

units.title: Parts of Speech
units.summary: Identify and correctly use nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, adverbs, prepositions, conjunctions, and interjections.

lessons.title: Nouns and Pronouns
lessons.intro: Every sentence needs something to talk about, and that job belongs to nouns and the pronouns that stand in for them. Get comfortable spotting both, and the rest of grammar, verbs matching subjects, pronouns agreeing with their nouns, starts falling into place.

sections.heading: Nouns: Naming People, Places, Things, and Ideas
body: A **noun** names a person, place, thing, or idea: teacher, kitchen, backpack, courage. **Common nouns** name general categories (city, dog, holiday) and are not capitalized. **Proper nouns** name specific, one-of-a-kind people, places, or things (Chicago, Rex, Thanksgiving) and are always capitalized.

Nouns also come in **singular** (one) and **plural** (more than one) forms, usually made by adding -s or -es: book/books, box/boxes. Some nouns break the pattern with irregular plurals, like child/children, mouse/mice, and person/people, these must be memorized rather than formed with a rule.

example.problem: Identify all the nouns in this sentence and label each common or proper: 'Maria walked her dog through the park on Saturday.'
steps: Find words naming a person, place, thing, or idea: Maria, dog, park, Saturday.
Maria and Saturday are specific, one-of-a-kind names, so they are proper nouns.
Dog and park are general categories, so they are common nouns.
example.answer: Proper nouns: Maria, Saturday. Common nouns: dog, park.

sections.heading: Pronouns: Standing In for Nouns
body: A **pronoun** replaces a noun so writing doesn't repeat the same word constantly. Instead of 'Jake grabbed Jake's coat because Jake was cold,' pronouns clean it up: 'Jake grabbed his coat because he was cold.' The noun a pronoun replaces is called its **antecedent**, here, Jake is the antecedent of both his and he.

Common pronoun types include **subject pronouns** (I, you, he, she, it, we, they), used as the doer of the action, and **object pronouns** (me, you, him, her, it, us, them), used as the receiver of the action. 'She called him' uses she as the subject and him as the object, swap them and the sentence means something entirely different.

example.problem: Rewrite this sentence using pronouns to avoid repeating the noun: 'Sarah finished Sarah's homework before Sarah went to bed.'
steps: Identify the repeated noun: Sarah.
Replace the second and third instances with the correct pronoun forms.
Sarah finished her homework before she went to bed.
example.answer: Sarah finished her homework before she went to bed.

keyTerms.def: A word that names a person, place, thing, or idea.
Common nouns name general categories; proper nouns name specific, capitalized things.
A word that replaces a noun, like he, she, it, or they.
The noun that a pronoun refers back to.

practice.q: Which word is a proper noun?
practice.explain: Paris names a specific, one-of-a-kind place, making it a proper noun that must be capitalized.

practice.q: In the sentence 'He gave her the book,' which word is an object pronoun?
practice.explain: 'Her' receives the action of the verb 'gave,' making it an object pronoun.

practice.q: What is the antecedent of 'it' in this sentence: 'The cat ate its food, then it slept'?
practice.explain: 'It' refers back to 'the cat,' which is its antecedent.

lessons.title: Verbs and Verb Tense
lessons.intro: If nouns are the actors in a sentence, verbs are what those actors do, and the tense of a verb tells your reader exactly when the action happened. Master verb tense and your writing gains a clear, confident timeline.

sections.heading: Action Verbs, Linking Verbs, and Helping Verbs
body: An **action verb** shows something a subject does: run, think, whisper, build. A **linking verb** connects the subject to a word that describes or renames it, without showing action; the most common linking verb is 'to be' (am, is, are, was, were). In 'The soup is hot,' is links 'soup' to the description 'hot,' nothing is being done, only described.

A **helping verb** works together with a main verb to build a complete verb phrase, showing tense or possibility. In 'She has finished her project,' has is the helping verb and finished is the main verb. Common helping verbs include has, have, had, is, are, was, will, and can.

example.problem: Identify the verb type in each sentence: (1) 'The dog barked loudly.' (2) 'The milk smells sour.'
steps: In sentence 1, barked shows an action the dog performed: an action verb.
In sentence 2, smells connects 'milk' to the description 'sour' rather than showing an action: a linking verb.
example.answer: (1) Action verb: barked. (2) Linking verb: smells.

sections.heading: Verb Tense: Past, Present, and Future
body: **Verb tense** tells when an action happens. **Present tense** describes what's happening now or generally true (I walk, she walks). **Past tense** describes something already finished, usually adding -ed to regular verbs (I walked). **Future tense** describes something yet to happen, usually formed with will (I will walk).

Irregular verbs don't follow the add -ed rule for past tense: go becomes went, not goed; eat becomes ate, not eated; see becomes saw, not seed. These irregular forms must be learned individually, since there's no shortcut formula that covers all of them.

example.problem: Change this sentence to past tense: 'She writes a letter every week.'
steps: Identify the present-tense verb: writes.
Recall that write is irregular in the past tense: write becomes wrote, not writed.
Rewrite: She wrote a letter every week.
example.answer: She wrote a letter every week.

keyTerms.def: A verb that shows something a subject does, like run or think.
A verb that connects the subject to a description or renaming, like 'is' or 'seems.'
A verb used with a main verb to form a complete verb phrase, showing tense or possibility.
The form of a verb showing when an action happens: past, present, or future.

practice.q: Which sentence uses a linking verb?
choices: The dog barked at the mailman.
practice.explain: 'Tastes' connects 'cake' to the description 'delicious' rather than showing an action, making it a linking verb.

practice.q: What is the past tense of the irregular verb 'go'?
practice.explain: 'Go' is irregular; its past tense is 'went,' not the regular -ed form.

practice.q: In 'They have finished the race,' what type of verb is 'have'?
practice.explain: 'Have' works with the main verb 'finished' to form a complete verb phrase, making it a helping verb.

lessons.title: Adjectives and Adverbs
lessons.intro: Nouns and verbs tell a story, but adjectives and adverbs are what make that story vivid, the difference between 'the dog ran' and 'the enormous, scruffy dog ran surprisingly fast.' Learn what each modifier can and can't describe.

sections.heading: Adjectives Describe Nouns
body: An **adjective** describes or modifies a noun or pronoun, answering questions like which one, what kind, or how many: the red bicycle, three cookies, a curious student. Adjectives usually sit right before the noun they describe, though they can also follow a linking verb, as in 'The bicycle is red.'

When comparing two things, add -er or use 'more' (taller, more difficult); when comparing three or more, add -est or use 'most' (tallest, most difficult). Short adjectives usually take -er/-est, while longer adjectives usually take more/most: fast → faster → fastest, but beautiful → more beautiful → most beautiful.

example.problem: Choose the correct comparative form: 'This puzzle is _____ than the last one.' (hard)
steps: 'Hard' is a short, one-syllable adjective.
Short adjectives typically take the -er ending for comparisons between two things.
The correct form is 'harder.'
example.answer: harder

sections.heading: Adverbs Describe Verbs, Adjectives, and Other Adverbs
body: An **adverb** modifies a verb, an adjective, or another adverb, answering how, when, where, or to what degree. Many adverbs end in -ly: quickly, carefully, silently. 'She ran quickly,' quickly modifies the verb ran, telling how she ran.

Adverbs can also modify adjectives or other adverbs to show degree: 'extremely hot' (extremely modifies the adjective hot) or 'very quickly' (very modifies the adverb quickly). A common mistake is using an adjective where an adverb belongs, as in 'She ran quick,' quick is an adjective, but a verb (ran) needs an adverb (quickly) to modify it.

example.problem: Correct the error: 'He speaks very calm during emergencies.'
steps: Identify what 'calm' is modifying: the verb 'speaks,' which needs an adverb, not an adjective.
Change the adjective 'calm' to the adverb form 'calmly.'
Corrected sentence: He speaks very calmly during emergencies.
example.answer: He speaks very calmly during emergencies.

keyTerms.def: A word that describes or modifies a noun or pronoun.
A word that modifies a verb, adjective, or another adverb, often ending in -ly.
Forms used to compare two things (-er/more) or three or more things (-est/most).

practice.q: Which word is an adjective in this sentence: 'The tall giraffe ate quietly'?
practice.explain: 'Tall' describes the noun 'giraffe,' making it an adjective.

practice.q: Which sentence uses the adverb correctly?
choices: She sang beautifully at the concert.
She sang beautiful at the concert.
practice.explain: 'Beautifully' correctly modifies the verb 'sang,' telling how she sang.

practice.q: What is the superlative form of 'good'?
practice.explain: 'Good' is irregular; its superlative form is 'best,' not a regular -est ending.

lessons.title: Prepositions, Conjunctions, and Interjections
lessons.intro: Three smaller parts of speech do some of grammar's biggest connecting work: prepositions link nouns to the rest of the sentence, conjunctions join ideas together, and interjections let raw emotion burst onto the page.

sections.heading: Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
body: A **preposition** shows the relationship between a noun (or pronoun) and another word in the sentence, often about location, direction, or time: in, on, at, under, before, after, between, through. A **prepositional phrase** starts with a preposition and ends with its noun or pronoun object: 'under the table,' 'before the meeting.'

Prepositional phrases usually act like adjectives or adverbs, adding detail. In 'The cat under the table is sleeping,' under the table describes which cat, like an adjective. In 'She arrived before the meeting,' before the meeting tells when she arrived, like an adverb.

example.problem: Identify the prepositional phrase in: 'The keys are on the kitchen counter.'
steps: Find the preposition: on.
Find the noun it connects to: kitchen counter.
The prepositional phrase is 'on the kitchen counter.'
example.answer: on the kitchen counter

sections.heading: Conjunctions and Interjections
body: A **conjunction** joins words, phrases, or clauses. **Coordinating conjunctions** (remembered by FANBOYS: for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) join equal parts, like two independent clauses: 'I studied, so I passed.' **Subordinating conjunctions** (because, although, if, when, since) join a dependent clause to an independent one: 'I passed because I studied.'

An **interjection** is a word or short phrase that expresses sudden emotion, standing mostly apart from the sentence's grammar: Wow!, Ouch!, Hey!, Yikes. Interjections are usually followed by an exclamation point or a comma and don't connect to anything grammatically, they just express feeling.

example.problem: Identify the conjunction and its type in: 'She wanted to go outside, but it was raining.'
steps: Find the joining word: but.
Check whether it joins two equal independent clauses or a dependent clause to an independent one.
It joins two independent clauses ('she wanted to go outside' and 'it was raining'), so it is a coordinating conjunction.
example.answer: 'But' is a coordinating conjunction.

keyTerms.def: A word showing the relationship between a noun and another word, like in, on, or under.
A preposition plus its noun or pronoun object, like 'under the table.'
A word that joins words, phrases, or clauses, like and, but, or because.
A word or phrase expressing sudden emotion, like Wow! or Ouch!

practice.q: Which word is a preposition in 'The book fell behind the couch'?
practice.explain: 'Behind' shows the relationship between the couch and where the book fell, making it a preposition.

practice.q: Which sentence uses a coordinating conjunction?
choices: I wanted pizza, but we ordered tacos.
Although it rained, we went hiking.
Because she was late, the meeting started without her.
When the bell rings, class begins.
practice.explain: 'But' joins two equal independent clauses, making it a coordinating conjunction; the other choices use subordinating conjunctions.

practice.q: Which word is an interjection?
practice.explain: 'Wow' expresses sudden emotion and stands apart from the sentence's grammar, making it an interjection.

units.title: Sentence Structure
units.summary: Identify subjects and predicates, build simple, compound, and complex sentences, and fix fragments and run-ons.

lessons.title: Subjects and Predicates
lessons.intro: Every complete sentence makes one basic promise: it names something and then says something about it. That two-part deal, subject and predicate, is the smallest unit of meaning in English, and spotting both halves instantly will make every other grammar rule easier to apply.

sections.heading: The Subject: Who or What the Sentence Is About
body: The **subject** of a sentence names who or what the sentence is about, and it's usually a noun or pronoun. The **simple subject** is just the key noun or pronoun (dog), while the **complete subject** includes all the words that describe it (The large, friendly dog).

To find the subject, ask 'who or what is doing something, or being described?' In 'The tired hikers finally reached the summit,' asking 'who reached the summit?' points to hikers as the simple subject, and 'the tired hikers' as the complete subject.

example.problem: Identify the simple subject and complete subject in: 'The old wooden bridge creaked under our feet.'
steps: Ask what the sentence is about: the bridge.
The simple subject is the single key noun: bridge.
The complete subject includes its describing words: 'the old wooden bridge.'
example.answer: Simple subject: bridge. Complete subject: the old wooden bridge.

sections.heading: The Predicate: What the Subject Does or Is
body: The **predicate** tells what the subject does or is, and it always contains the verb. The **simple predicate** is just the verb (creaked), while the **complete predicate** includes the verb plus everything that goes with it (creaked under our feet).

A sentence is only complete when it has both a subject and a predicate that make a full thought. 'The dog' is not a complete sentence, it has a subject but no predicate, so it leaves the reader waiting to know what the dog did or is.

example.problem: Identify the simple predicate and complete predicate in: 'The students quickly finished their test.'
steps: Find the verb: finished.
The simple predicate is just that verb: finished.
The complete predicate includes everything describing the action: 'quickly finished their test.'
example.answer: Simple predicate: finished. Complete predicate: quickly finished their test.

keyTerms.def: The part of a sentence naming who or what it is about.
The part of a sentence telling what the subject does or is, containing the verb.
A sentence containing both a subject and a predicate that express a full thought.

practice.q: What is the simple subject in 'The three young puppies played in the yard'?
practice.explain: 'Puppies' is the key noun the sentence is about; the describing words form the complete subject.

practice.q: What is the simple predicate in 'My sister carefully wrapped the gift'?
practice.explain: 'Wrapped' is the verb, making it the simple predicate.

practice.q: Why is 'Running down the street' not a complete sentence?
practice.explain: 'Running down the street' has an action but no subject telling who or what is running, so it's incomplete.

lessons.title: Simple, Compound, and Complex Sentences
lessons.intro: Varying your sentence length and structure is one of the fastest ways to make writing sound more mature, and it starts with knowing the difference between a simple, compound, and complex sentence, and when to reach for each.

sections.heading: Simple and Compound Sentences
body: A **simple sentence** has exactly one independent clause: one subject-predicate pair expressing a complete thought, like 'The rain stopped.' It can still have extra description, like 'The heavy rain finally stopped after lunch,' and remain simple, because it still contains only one independent clause.

A **compound sentence** joins two independent clauses with a coordinating conjunction (FANBOYS) or a semicolon: 'The rain stopped, and the sun came out' or 'The rain stopped; the sun came out.' Each half could stand alone as its own sentence, which is exactly what makes it 'compound' rather than 'complex.'

example.problem: Combine these two simple sentences into one compound sentence: 'I wanted to go for a walk. It started to rain.'
steps: Identify that both are independent clauses that could stand alone.
Choose a coordinating conjunction that fits the logical relationship: but (contrast).
Combine with a comma before the conjunction: 'I wanted to go for a walk, but it started to rain.'
example.answer: I wanted to go for a walk, but it started to rain.

sections.heading: Complex Sentences
body: A **complex sentence** joins one independent clause with at least one **dependent clause** (a clause that can't stand alone), connected by a subordinating conjunction like because, although, when, since, or if. 'Although it started to rain, I went for a walk' has the dependent clause 'Although it started to rain' attached to the independent clause 'I went for a walk.'

When the dependent clause comes first, it's followed by a comma: 'Because she studied hard, she passed the test.' When the independent clause comes first, usually no comma is needed: 'She passed the test because she studied hard.' Noticing which clause leads tells you whether the comma belongs.

example.problem: Combine using a subordinating conjunction: 'She finished her homework. She watched a movie.' (Use 'after')
steps: Decide which idea is dependent and which leads: 'After she finished her homework' can be the dependent clause.
Attach it to the independent clause: 'she watched a movie.'
Since the dependent clause comes first, add a comma: 'After she finished her homework, she watched a movie.'
example.answer: After she finished her homework, she watched a movie.

keyTerms.def: A sentence with exactly one independent clause.
Two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction or semicolon.
An independent clause joined with at least one dependent clause.
An independent clause can stand alone; a dependent clause cannot.

practice.q: Which sentence is compound?
choices: The wind howled, and the trees bent.
The wind howled loudly all night.
Because the wind howled, we stayed inside.
practice.explain: Two independent clauses ('the wind howled' and 'the trees bent') are joined by the coordinating conjunction 'and,' making this compound.

practice.q: Which sentence is complex?
choices: Although the wind howled, we slept soundly.
The wind howled, and we slept soundly.
We slept through the howling wind.
practice.explain: The dependent clause 'Although the wind howled' is joined to the independent clause 'we slept soundly,' making this complex.

practice.q: In 'Because it was cold, we lit a fire,' what type of clause is 'Because it was cold'?
practice.explain: 'Because it was cold' cannot stand alone as a complete sentence, making it a dependent clause.

lessons.title: Fixing Fragments and Run-ons
lessons.intro: Two of the most common sentence errors sit at opposite extremes: the fragment says too little to stand alone, and the run-on crams too much together without a pause. Learn to spot and fix both, and your sentences will read cleanly every time.

sections.heading: Sentence Fragments
body: A **sentence fragment** is an incomplete sentence punctuated as if it were complete, it's missing a subject, a predicate, or both, or it's a dependent clause standing alone. 'Running through the park.' is a fragment: it has no subject doing the running.

To fix a fragment, either add the missing piece or attach it to a nearby complete sentence. 'Running through the park.' becomes complete as 'She was running through the park,' or it can attach to a full sentence: 'She waved at me, running through the park.'

example.problem: Fix this fragment: 'Because she forgot her umbrella.'
steps: Recognize that this is a dependent clause, not a complete sentence, because it starts with the subordinating conjunction 'because.'
Attach it to an independent clause to complete the thought.
Corrected: 'Because she forgot her umbrella, she got soaked in the rain.'
example.answer: Because she forgot her umbrella, she got soaked in the rain.

sections.heading: Run-on Sentences and Comma Splices
body: A **run-on sentence** happens when two or more independent clauses are jammed together with no punctuation or connecting word: 'I love pizza I eat it every week.' A **comma splice** is a specific type of run-on that uses only a comma to join two independent clauses: 'I love pizza, I eat it every week.'

Fix a run-on in one of four ways: split it into two sentences with a period, add a coordinating conjunction after a comma, replace the comma with a semicolon, or add a subordinating conjunction. 'I love pizza, I eat it every week' can become 'I love pizza, and I eat it every week,' or 'I love pizza; I eat it every week.'

example.problem: Fix this run-on: 'The movie was long it was still enjoyable.'
steps: Identify the two independent clauses: 'The movie was long' and 'it was still enjoyable.'
Choose a fix: add a comma and coordinating conjunction that shows contrast.
Corrected: 'The movie was long, but it was still enjoyable.'
example.answer: The movie was long, but it was still enjoyable.

keyTerms.def: An incomplete sentence punctuated as if it were complete.
Two or more independent clauses jammed together with no punctuation or connecting word.
A run-on that uses only a comma to join two independent clauses.

practice.q: Which of these is a sentence fragment?
choices: She walks to school every morning.
practice.explain: This phrase has no subject performing the action and no complete predicate, making it a fragment.

practice.q: Which sentence is a comma splice?
choices: I finished my homework, I watched TV.
I finished my homework, and I watched TV.
I finished my homework before I watched TV.
I finished my homework; I watched TV.
practice.explain: Two independent clauses are joined with only a comma and no conjunction, which is a comma splice.

practice.q: What is the best fix for the run-on 'She was tired she kept working'?
choices: She was tired, but she kept working.
She was tired she kept, working.
She was, tired she kept working.
practice.explain: Adding a comma and the coordinating conjunction 'but' correctly joins the two independent clauses.

units.title: Punctuation and Capitalization
units.summary: Master the rules for end punctuation, commas, apostrophes, quotation marks, colons, semicolons, and capitalization.

lessons.title: End Punctuation and Commas
lessons.intro: Punctuation is the traffic signal system of writing, it tells the reader when to stop, when to pause, and what kind of sentence they just finished reading. Get the basics of end marks and commas right, and your sentences instantly become easier to follow.

sections.heading: End Punctuation: Periods, Question Marks, and Exclamation Points
body: A **period** ends a statement or a command: 'The store closes at nine.' 'Close the door.' A **question mark** ends a direct question: 'What time does the store close?' An **exclamation point** ends a sentence expressing strong emotion or emphasis: 'Watch out!'

Exclamation points lose their punch if overused, reserve them for genuine urgency or excitement, not for every sentence you want to emphasize. A whole paragraph of exclamation points reads as less intense than one used sparingly at the exact right moment.

sections.heading: Commas: Lists, Introductions, and Joining Clauses
body: Use a comma to separate items in a list of three or more: 'I bought apples, bananas, and grapes.' Use a comma after an introductory word, phrase, or clause: 'After the game, we grabbed dinner.' Use a comma before a coordinating conjunction joining two independent clauses: 'I was tired, but I finished the race.'

A common mistake is placing a comma between just a subject and its verb, which should never happen: 'My best friend, loves hiking' is wrong; it should be 'My best friend loves hiking' with no comma at all, since there's no list, introduction, or joined clause to justify one.

example.problem: Add commas where needed: 'After the storm passed we cleaned up the yard and repaired the fence.'
steps: Find the introductory clause: 'After the storm passed' needs a comma after it.
Check for a list or joined independent clauses in the rest: the remaining part is one clause with a compound verb, so no additional comma is needed there.
Corrected: 'After the storm passed, we cleaned up the yard and repaired the fence.'
example.answer: After the storm passed, we cleaned up the yard and repaired the fence.

keyTerms.def: The end mark for a statement or command.
The end mark for a direct question.
The end mark for a sentence showing strong emotion or emphasis.
A punctuation mark used to separate list items, follow introductions, or join independent clauses.

practice.q: Which sentence uses commas correctly in a list?
choices: I need bread, milk, and eggs.
I need bread milk, and eggs.
I need, bread, milk and eggs.
I need bread, milk and, eggs.
practice.explain: Commas correctly separate each of the three list items: bread, milk, and eggs.

practice.q: Which sentence needs a comma after the introductory phrase?
choices: After dinner we washed the dishes.
We washed the dishes after dinner.
The dishes were washed after dinner.
practice.explain: 'After dinner' is an introductory phrase and needs a comma after it: 'After dinner, we washed the dishes.'

practice.q: Which sentence uses an exclamation point correctly?
choices: The book is on the table!
practice.explain: 'Watch out for that car!' expresses genuine urgency, which is the appropriate use for an exclamation point.

lessons.title: Apostrophes, Quotation Marks, and Colons/Semicolons
lessons.intro: These four punctuation marks handle some of writing's trickiest jobs: showing ownership, marking exact spoken words, and connecting closely related ideas. Mixing them up is one of the most common errors even confident writers make.

sections.heading: Apostrophes: Possession and Contractions
body: An **apostrophe** shows possession or marks a contraction. For possession, add 's to singular nouns (the dog's leash) and most singular names, even ones ending in s (James's book). For plural nouns already ending in s, add just an apostrophe (the dogs' leashes, meaning more than one dog).

For **contractions**, the apostrophe replaces missing letters: do not becomes don't, it is becomes it's, they are becomes they're. A frequent mix-up: 'its' (possessive, no apostrophe, meaning belonging to it) versus 'it's' (contraction of it is or it has). 'The dog wagged its tail' needs no apostrophe; 'It's raining' does.

example.problem: Choose the correct word: 'The company changed _____ logo last year.' (its/it's)
steps: Determine whether the sentence needs the possessive form or the contraction of 'it is.'
The sentence means 'belonging to the company,' which calls for the possessive.
The possessive form of it has no apostrophe: its.
example.answer: its

sections.heading: Quotation Marks, Colons, and Semicolons
body: **Quotation marks** enclose someone's exact spoken or written words: She said, 'I'll be there at noon.' Commas and periods usually go inside the closing quotation mark in American English. A **colon** introduces a list, explanation, or quotation after a complete independent clause: 'Bring three things: a jacket, water, and a map.'

A **semicolon** joins two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction, acting as a stronger pause than a comma but a softer break than a period: 'The forecast called for rain; we brought umbrellas just in case.' Semicolons can also separate items in a complex list that already contains commas.

example.problem: Punctuate correctly: 'She had one goal finish the marathon'
steps: Recognize that 'She had one goal' is a complete independent clause introducing an explanation.
A colon is the right mark to introduce that explanation after a complete clause.
Corrected: 'She had one goal: finish the marathon.'
example.answer: She had one goal: finish the marathon.

keyTerms.def: A mark showing possession (dog's) or replacing missing letters in a contraction (don't).
Marks enclosing someone's exact spoken or written words.
A mark introducing a list, explanation, or quotation after a complete clause.
A mark joining two closely related independent clauses without a conjunction.

practice.q: Which sentence uses 'its' correctly?
practice.explain: 'Its' shows possession (the wings belonging to the bird) and needs no apostrophe, unlike the contraction 'it's.'

practice.q: Which sentence correctly uses a colon?
choices: Pack these items: a tent, a flashlight, and food.
Pack these items, a tent a flashlight and food.
Pack: these items a tent a flashlight and food.
Pack these: items a tent, a flashlight, and food.
practice.explain: The colon correctly follows the complete independent clause 'Pack these items' to introduce the list.

practice.q: Which sentence correctly uses a semicolon?
choices: The sky darkened; a storm was coming.
The sky darkened, a storm was coming; soon.
The sky; darkened a storm was coming.
The sky darkened a storm; was coming.
practice.explain: The semicolon correctly joins two closely related independent clauses: 'The sky darkened' and 'a storm was coming.'

lessons.title: Capitalization Rules
lessons.intro: Capital letters aren't decoration, each one signals something specific to the reader: a new sentence starting, a proper name appearing, or a title being referenced. Master the rules and your writing looks polished at a glance.

sections.heading: Capitalizing Sentences, Names, and Places
body: Always capitalize the first word of every sentence, and the pronoun 'I' no matter where it appears in a sentence. Capitalize **proper nouns**: specific people (Maria), specific places (Tokyo, Yellowstone National Park), specific organizations (NASA), and specific things (the Golden Gate Bridge).

Titles that come directly before a name are capitalized, like Doctor Chen or President Lincoln, but the same word is lowercase when used generally: 'I have an appointment with the doctor' or 'the president gave a speech.' The rule is about specificity, not the word itself.

sections.heading: Capitalizing Titles, Days, and Directions
body: In titles of books, movies, and articles, capitalize the first word, the last word, and every important word in between, but leave small connecting words lowercase (a, an, the, and, of, in) unless they start or end the title: 'The Lord of the Rings,' 'A Wrinkle in Time.'

Capitalize days of the week, months, and holidays (Monday, October, Thanksgiving), but not seasons (summer, winter) unless a season starts a sentence. Capitalize direction words only when they name a specific region (the Midwest, the South), not when they simply indicate direction (drive west, turn south).

example.problem: Correct the capitalization: 'my aunt visited yellowstone national park last summer with dr. lin.'
steps: Capitalize the first word of the sentence: My.
Capitalize the proper noun (specific place): Yellowstone National Park.
Capitalize the title before a name: Dr. Lin.
Leave 'summer' lowercase, since it's a season, not a proper noun.
example.answer: My aunt visited Yellowstone National Park last summer with Dr. Lin.

keyTerms.def: Specific people, places, organizations, and things are always capitalized.
Capitalize the first word, last word, and important words in a title.
Capitalize direction words only when they name a specific region, like the Midwest.

practice.q: Which sentence is correctly capitalized?
choices: We visited Yellowstone National Park in July.
We visited yellowstone national Park in july.
we visited Yellowstone national park in July.
We visited Yellowstone National park In July.
practice.explain: The proper noun 'Yellowstone National Park' and the month 'July' are both correctly capitalized, with the sentence starting capitalized too.

practice.q: Which use of a title is correctly capitalized?
choices: I have an appointment with Doctor Chen.
I have an appointment with the Doctor.
I have an appointment with doctor Chen.
I have an appointment with the doctor Chen.
practice.explain: 'Doctor Chen' capitalizes the title because it comes directly before a specific name.

practice.q: Which direction word should be capitalized?
practice.explain: 'The Midwest' names a specific region, so it is capitalized, unlike direction words used generally.

units.title: Building Paragraphs
units.summary: Construct unified paragraphs with strong topic sentences, supporting details, and smooth transitions.

lessons.title: Topic Sentences and Supporting Details
lessons.intro: A paragraph without a clear topic sentence is like a road trip without a destination, the reader has no idea where you're headed or why each detail matters. Learn to build a paragraph around one strong controlling idea.

sections.heading: The Topic Sentence
body: A **topic sentence** states the single main idea of a paragraph, usually as the first sentence, and every other sentence in the paragraph should support or explain it. A strong topic sentence is specific enough to guide the paragraph, not so broad it could apply to almost anything: 'Dogs make great pets' is vague, while 'Dogs make great pets for busy families because they adapt easily to a routine' points toward exactly what the paragraph will prove.

Everything in the paragraph should trace back to the topic sentence. If a sentence about a dog's grooming needs suddenly appears in a paragraph about dogs adapting to family routines, it's a sign that sentence belongs somewhere else, or the topic sentence needs to be broadened to include it.

sections.heading: Supporting Details
body: **Supporting details** are the specific facts, examples, and explanations that back up the topic sentence. Vague supporting sentences ('Dogs are good for families') repeat the main idea without adding anything new; strong supporting details add concrete evidence ('A dog can be walked in the same 20 minutes each morning, fitting easily around a work schedule').

A well-built paragraph typically includes 3-5 supporting details, each expanding the topic sentence with a different angle: an example, a statistic, a comparison, or a small story. Ending with a **concluding sentence** that restates the main idea in new words gives the paragraph a sense of closure.

example.problem: Given the topic sentence 'Recycling paper conserves natural resources,' which of these details best supports it: (a) 'Paper recycling bins are usually blue,' or (b) 'Recycling one ton of paper saves about 17 trees'?
steps: Check whether each detail actually supports the claim about conserving resources.
The bin color (a) has nothing to do with conserving resources.
The statistic about trees saved (b) directly supports the claim with concrete evidence.
example.answer: (b) 'Recycling one ton of paper saves about 17 trees' is the stronger supporting detail.

keyTerms.def: The sentence stating the single main idea of a paragraph.
A specific fact, example, or explanation that backs up the topic sentence.
The final sentence restating the main idea and giving the paragraph closure.

practice.q: Which is the best topic sentence for a paragraph about the benefits of morning exercise?
choices: Morning exercise boosts energy and focus for the rest of the day.
Mornings can be busy for everyone.
practice.explain: This sentence states a specific, provable main idea that the rest of the paragraph can support with details.

practice.q: In a paragraph about the benefits of libraries, which sentence is an irrelevant detail?
choices: The librarian's favorite color is green.
Libraries offer free access to thousands of books.
Libraries often host free community events.
practice.explain: A librarian's favorite color has nothing to do with the benefits of libraries, breaking the paragraph's focus.

practice.q: What is the purpose of a concluding sentence?
choices: To restate the main idea in new words and give the paragraph closure
To introduce a brand new topic
practice.explain: A concluding sentence wraps up the paragraph by restating its main idea, giving the reader a sense of closure.

lessons.title: Transitions and Paragraph Unity
lessons.intro: Ideas need bridges. Without transition words, a paragraph reads like a list of disconnected facts; with them, one idea flows logically into the next, and the reader can follow your thinking instead of guessing at it.

sections.heading: Using Transition Words
body: **Transitions** are words and phrases that show the relationship between ideas. Some add information (also, in addition, furthermore), some show contrast (however, on the other hand, but), some show cause and effect (therefore, as a result, because), and some show sequence (first, next, finally).

Choosing the right transition depends on the logical relationship, not just variety for its own sake. Writing 'It rained all day. However, we finished the hike' correctly signals contrast between the rain and finishing anyway; swapping in 'Therefore' would confuse the reader, since finishing the hike wasn't caused by the rain.

example.problem: Choose the best transition: 'The bridge was closed for repairs. _____, we had to take a longer route home.'
steps: Identify the logical relationship: the closed bridge caused the need for a longer route.
A cause-and-effect transition fits this relationship.
'As a result' correctly signals that the detour is a consequence of the closure.
example.answer: As a result

sections.heading: Paragraph Unity
body: **Paragraph unity** means every sentence works together to develop one main idea, without wandering off-topic. A unified paragraph reads like a single, connected argument or story, not a grab-bag of loosely related sentences.

To check unity, reread each sentence and ask whether it directly supports the topic sentence. If a sentence introduces a genuinely new idea, it usually belongs in its own paragraph, with its own topic sentence, rather than being squeezed into the current one.

keyTerms.def: A word or phrase showing the relationship between ideas, like however or therefore.
A transition signaling that one idea caused another, like therefore or as a result.
The quality of every sentence in a paragraph supporting one main idea.

practice.q: Which transition best shows contrast?
practice.explain: 'However' signals a contrast between two ideas, unlike the other options which show addition, sequence, or cause.

practice.q: Which transition fits: 'She studied hard every night. _____, she earned the highest grade in the class.'
practice.explain: 'As a result' signals that her high grade was a consequence of her studying, a cause-and-effect relationship.

practice.q: A paragraph about ocean pollution suddenly includes a sentence about a favorite vacation spot with no ocean connection. What does this break?
practice.explain: An unrelated sentence breaks paragraph unity, since it doesn't support the paragraph's main idea about ocean pollution.

units.title: The Writing Process and Style
units.summary: Move a piece of writing through prewriting, drafting, revising, and editing, and sharpen word choice and tone.

lessons.title: Planning, Drafting, and Revising
lessons.intro: Good writing is rarely good on the first try, it's the product of a process: plan before you write, draft without stopping to perfect every sentence, and then revise with a critical eye. Skipping straight to a 'final' draft usually shows.

sections.heading: Prewriting and Drafting
body: **Prewriting** is the planning stage before you write a single full sentence: brainstorming ideas, choosing a focus, and organizing thoughts into a rough outline. A simple outline for an essay might list a main claim followed by three supporting points, each with one or two pieces of evidence.

**Drafting** means writing a full first version without stopping to perfect every word choice or worry about small errors. The goal of a first draft is to get the whole structure down on paper; polishing comes later, in revision. Writers who try to perfect every sentence during drafting often get stuck and never finish.

sections.heading: Revising vs. Editing
body: **Revising** means reworking the big-picture elements: does the argument make sense, are ideas in the best order, is anything missing or unnecessary, does each paragraph support the main point? Revising can mean deleting whole paragraphs, adding new evidence, or reordering sections.

**Editing** comes after revising and focuses on smaller, sentence-level fixes: grammar, spelling, punctuation, and word choice. Doing these out of order, editing sentences before the big-picture structure is settled, often wastes effort polishing sentences that get cut once the structure changes.

example.problem: A student has finished a first draft of an essay but the third paragraph doesn't connect to the main argument at all. Should the student revise or edit first, and why?
steps: Identify the type of problem: it's a structural issue, not a small sentence-level error.
Structural problems belong to revision, which comes before editing.
The student should revise first, deciding whether to rewrite, move, or cut the paragraph, before editing individual sentences within it.
example.answer: Revise first, since the issue is structural (paragraph relevance), not a small grammar or word-choice error.

keyTerms.def: The planning stage before drafting: brainstorming, focusing, and outlining ideas.
Writing a full first version of a piece without stopping to perfect it.
Reworking a draft's big-picture structure, argument, and organization.
Fixing smaller sentence-level issues like grammar, spelling, and punctuation.

practice.q: What is the main purpose of prewriting?
choices: To plan and organize ideas before writing a full draft
practice.explain: Prewriting is the planning stage where ideas are brainstormed and organized before the actual drafting begins.

practice.q: Which task belongs to revising rather than editing?
choices: Reordering paragraphs so the argument flows logically
practice.explain: Reordering paragraphs is a big-picture, structural change, which belongs to revising rather than sentence-level editing.

practice.q: Why should editing usually happen after revising, not before?
choices: Because polishing sentences that might get cut during revision wastes effort
Because revising always comes last in the process
Because editing must happen before any writing begins
practice.explain: If big structural changes happen during revision, sentences polished beforehand may get cut or reworked, wasting the editing effort.

lessons.title: Word Choice, Tone, and Avoiding Wordiness
lessons.intro: The same idea can sound flat, sound false, or sound exactly right, depending on the words you pick. This lesson sharpens three tools: choosing precise words, matching your tone to your audience, and cutting the clutter that dilutes a strong sentence.

sections.heading: Precise Word Choice
body: Vague words force readers to fill in the blanks themselves. 'The weather was bad' tells the reader almost nothing; 'The freezing rain turned the sidewalk to ice' paints an exact picture. Choosing specific nouns and strong verbs almost always beats piling on extra adjectives.

Strong verbs can replace weak verb-plus-adverb combinations. Instead of 'walked quickly,' consider 'hurried' or 'dashed'; instead of 'said loudly,' consider 'shouted' or 'exclaimed.' One precise verb usually carries more information and more energy than a generic verb propped up by an adverb.

sections.heading: Tone and Cutting Wordiness
body: **Tone** is the attitude a piece of writing takes toward its subject and audience, formal, casual, humorous, serious. A text message to a friend and an email to a teacher can describe the exact same experience with completely different, appropriate tones.

**Wordiness** happens when extra words pad a sentence without adding meaning. 'Due to the fact that it was raining, we decided to cancel the picnic' can be trimmed to 'Because it was raining, we canceled the picnic,' same meaning, fewer words, more impact. Watch for padded phrases like 'due to the fact that,' 'in order to,' and 'at this point in time,' which usually shrink to one word each: because, to, now.

example.problem: Revise for concision: 'At this point in time, we are of the opinion that the plan needs revision.'
steps: Find the padded phrase 'at this point in time' and replace it with 'now' or cut it.
Find 'are of the opinion that' and replace it with the simpler 'think.'
Revised: 'We think the plan needs revision.'
example.answer: We think the plan needs revision.

keyTerms.def: The attitude a piece of writing takes toward its subject and audience.
Selecting specific, exact words instead of vague or generic ones.
Extra words that pad a sentence without adding meaning.
Expressing an idea clearly using no more words than necessary.

practice.q: Which sentence uses the most precise verb?
choices: She sprinted to the bus stop.
She went quickly to the bus stop.
She moved to the bus stop fast.
She got to the bus stop rapidly.
practice.explain: 'Sprinted' is a single, precise verb that conveys speed on its own, unlike the other choices that pair a weak verb with an adverb.

practice.q: Which revision best fixes wordiness in 'Due to the fact that he was tired, he went to bed early'?
choices: Because he was tired, he went to bed early.
Due to being tired, to bed early he went.
He was tired, due to the fact of going to bed early.
Because of the fact he was tired he went to bed.
practice.explain: Replacing the padded phrase 'due to the fact that' with the single word 'because' keeps the same meaning with far fewer words.

practice.q: A student writes a text to a friend using very formal, academic language. What issue does this show?
choices: A mismatch between tone and audience
practice.explain: Using overly formal language in a casual text to a friend shows a mismatch between tone and the intended audience.
